topics.title: Congruence of Triangles and Criteria for Congruence
topics.concept:
What is Congruence of Triangles?

In simple English, congruence means identical in every single way. If two shapes have the exact same shape and the exact same size, they are said to be congruent.

Imagine two identical brand-new one-rupee coins placed directly on top of each other. They cover each other completely because their boundaries match perfectly. In geometry, when two triangles are congruent, it means that if you cut one out and place it over the other, it will cover it exactly.

When two triangles, Triangle ABC and Triangle PQR, are congruent, we write it using the special symbol "≅":

Triangle ABC ≅ Triangle PQR

This symbol combines "~" (same shape) and "=" (same size).

When two triangles are congruent, their corresponding parts match up perfectly. This gives us a very important rule called CPCT, which stands for Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles. This means:

  • Corresponding sides are equal.
  • Corresponding angles are equal.

Instead of measuring all three sides and all three angles every time, mathematicians discovered four main shortcut rules or criteria for congruence:

  1. SAS (Side-Angle-Side): Two triangles are congruent if two sides and the included angle of one triangle are equal to two sides and the included angle of the other triangle. (Note: The angle must be trapped tightly between the two sides).
  2. ASA (Angle-Side-Angle): Two triangles are congruent if two angles and the included side of one triangle are equal to two angles and the included side of the other triangle.
  3. SSS (Side-Side-Side): Two triangles are congruent if all three sides of one triangle are equal to the corresponding three sides of the other triangle.
  4. RHS (Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side): Two right-angled triangles are congruent if the hypotenuse and one side of one triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and one side of the other triangle.

Let us look at a quick comparison table of these rules:

Congruence RuleFull NameWhat Must Be Equal?Position Rule
**ASA**Angle-Side-Angle2 Angles and 1 SideThe side must be *between* the two angles.
**SSS**Side-Side-Side3 SidesAll three matching pairs of sides must be equal.
**RHS**Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side1 Right Angle, Hypotenuse, 1 SideApplies only to right-angled triangles.

topics.title: Properties of a Triangle—Angles and Sides
topics.concept:
What are the Properties of a Triangle's Angles and Sides?

Triangles have beautiful internal mathematical relationships connecting their sides and angles. When you change the length of a side, the angle opposite to it changes too.

Here are the fundamental rules governing these properties:

  1. Isosceles Triangle Property: An isosceles triangle is a triangle that has two equal sides. The rule states that the angles opposite to the equal sides of an isosceles triangle are also equal. For example, if side AB = side AC in Triangle ABC, then Angle B (opposite side AC) must equal Angle C (opposite side AB).
  2. Converse of Isosceles Property: If two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite to those equal angles must also be equal in length.
  3. Equilateral Triangle Property: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal. Because all sides are equal, all three internal angles must also be equal to one another. Since the total sum of angles in a triangle is always 180°, each angle of an equilateral triangle measures exactly 60° (180° divided by 3).

Let us check how these properties look:

Triangle TypeSide ConditionAngle ConditionSpecial Value
**Equilateral**All three sides are equalAll three angles are equalEach angle is always 60°
**Scalene**No sides are equalNo angles are equalAll angles are different

What are the Properties of a Triangle's Angles and Sides?

Triangles have beautiful internal mathematical relationships connecting their sides and angles. When you change the length of a side, the angle opposite to it changes too.

Here are the fundamental rules governing these properties:

1. Isosceles Triangle Property: An isosceles triangle is a triangle that has two equal sides. The rule states that the angles opposite to the equal sides of an isosceles triangle are also equal. For example, if side AB = side AC in Triangle ABC, then Angle B (opposite side AC) must equal Angle C (opposite side AB). 2. Converse of Isosceles Property: If two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite to those equal angles must also be equal in length. 3. Equilateral Triangle Property: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal. Because all sides are equal, all three internal angles must also be equal to one another. Since the total sum of angles in a triangle is always 180°, each angle of an equilateral triangle measures exactly 60° (180° divided by 3).

Let us check how these properties look:

Triangle TypeSide ConditionAngle ConditionSpecial Value
------------
IsoscelesTwo sides are equalTwo angles opposite to those sides are equalVaries
EquilateralAll three sides are equalAll three angles are equalEach angle is always 60°

     Side/     \Side
    AB  /       \AC
       /         \
      /___________\
     B             C
     Angle B = Angle C
     (Angles opposite to equal sides AB and AC)

points: In an **isosceles triangle**, angles opposite to equal sides are always equal.
Conversely, if two angles of a triangle are equal, the sides opposite to them must be equal.
An **equilateral triangle** has three equal sides and three equal angles, with each angle measuring exactly 60°.
The sum of all interior angles of any triangle is always 180°.
You can use congruence rules like SAS to prove that specific line segments or angles inside a triangle are equal via CPCT.

topics.title: Inequalities in a Triangle
topics.concept:
What are Triangle Inequalities?

In the previous topic, we looked at what happens when sides and angles are perfectly equal. But what happens when they are not equal? Inequalities deal with relationships of "greater than" (>) or "less than" (<).

There are two major laws that govern inequalities in triangles:

  1. The Side-Angle Inequality Theorem: If two sides of a triangle are unequal in length, the angle opposite to the longer side is always larger than the angle opposite to the shorter side. Think of it like a crane or a laptop lid: the wider you open the angle, the longer the distance between the tips becomes! Conversely, the side opposite to the larger angle is always the longer side.
  2. The Triangle Inequality Theorem: This is a fundamental rule of nature. It states that the sum of the lengths of any two sides of a triangle must be strictly greater than the length of the third side. If this rule is broken, the two sides will lie flat or won't reach each other, and you cannot form a closed triangle at all!

Let us see how the Triangle Inequality Theorem works with an example. Suppose a triangle has sides of length \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\). For this triangle to exist, all three of these conditions must be true:

  • \(a + b > c\)
  • \(b + c > a\)
  • \(a + c > b\)

A helpful shortcut rule derived from this is: The difference between any two sides of a triangle is always less than the third side (\(|a - b| < c\)).

     3  /  \ 4     Side 3 + Side 4 = 7, which is > 5.
       /____\      Triangle forms perfectly!
         5

  Case B: Sum of two sides is too short (Invalid)
     3        2
   /            \   
  /______________\  Side 3 + Side 2 = 5, which is equal to 6.
         6          The ends cannot touch to form a corner!
                    No triangle can be made.

points: In any triangle, the angle opposite to the **longer side** is always **larger**.
Conversely, the side opposite to the **larger angle** is always **longer**.
The **Triangle Inequality Theorem** states that the sum of any two sides of a triangle must be strictly greater than the third side ($a + b > c$).
If the sum of the two smaller side lengths is equal to or less than the largest side length, a triangle **cannot** be formed.
The difference between any two side lengths of a triangle is always less than the length of the third side.

questions.q: If Triangle ABC ≅ Triangle PQR by SSS congruence rule, then which of the following is true?
options: AB = PQ, BC = QR, AC = PR
AB = QR, BC = PR, AC = PQ
AB = PR, BC = PQ, AC = QR
questions.explanation: SSS requires all three corresponding pairs of matching sides to be equal.

questions.q: In Triangle ABC, if AB = AC and Angle B = 50°, what is the measure of Angle A?
questions.explanation: Angle C = Angle B = 50°. Sum is 180°, so Angle A = 180° - 100° = 80°.

questions.q: Which of the following sets of side lengths can form a valid triangle?
questions.explanation: Only 5 + 6 > 10 satisfies the triangle inequality rule for all combinations.

questions.q: In Triangle PQR, if Angle P = 60° and Angle Q = 40°, which side is the longest?
questions.explanation: Angle R = 180° - (60° + 40°) = 80°. The longest side is opposite to Angle R, which is PQ.

questions.q: For two triangles to be congruent by the SAS rule, the equal angle must be:
questions.explanation: The definition of SAS requires the angle to be trapped between the two sides.

questions.q: In Triangle ABC, if AB = 7 cm, BC = 8 cm, and AC = 6 cm, which angle is the smallest?
questions.explanation: The smallest angle is opposite to the shortest side, which is AC (6 cm).

questions.q: If the hypotenuse and a side of one right triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and a side of another right triangle, the triangles are congruent by:
questions.explanation: This matches the definition of the Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side (RHS) rule.

questions.q: In an isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC, if AD is a perpendicular line drawn from A to BC, then:
questions.explanation: Triangle ABD ≅ Triangle ACD by RHS, so BD = CD by CPCT.

questions.q: What is the measure of each interior angle of an equilateral triangle?
questions.explanation: Since all three sides are equal, 180° divided by 3 gives exactly 60° per angle.

questions.q: If two sides of a triangle measure 4 cm and 7 cm, the third side length must be:
questions.explanation: Sum rule: side < 4+7=11. Difference rule: side > 7-4=3. So it must be between 3 and 11.

questions.q: In Triangle ABC, the bisectors of interior Angle B and exterior Angle C intersect at point P. If Angle A = 50°, find the measure of Angle BPC.
questions.explanation: By using exterior angle theorems, it can be proven that Angle BPC is always half of Angle A.

questions.q: Point O is an interior point of a Triangle ABC. Which of the following inequality relations is always true for any triangle?
options: OA + OB + OC < AB + BC + CA
OA + OB + OC > AB + BC + CA
OA + OB + OC = AB + BC + CA
questions.explanation: Summing the inequalities of triangles OAB, OBC, and OCA gives 2(OA+OB+OC) > AB+BC+CA.

questions.q: In a triangle, the lengths of two sides are 6 cm and 13 cm. If the third side length is an integer '$x$', find the number of possible integer values that '$x$' can take.
questions.explanation: $13 - 6 < x < 13 + 6$, so $7 < x < 19$. The integers are 8 to 18, which gives 11 values.

questions.q: In Triangle ABC, AD is the median drawn to side BC. Which of the following structural statements is always true?
questions.explanation: Extend AD to E such that AD=DE. Triangle ABD≅ECD implies AC+EC > AE, so AB+AC > 2AD.

questions.q: In right-angled Triangle ABC (with Angle B = 90°), P and Q are points on sides AB and BC respectively. Choose the correct relation regarding the hypotenuse splits:
questions.explanation: Apply the Pythagoras theorem to triangles ABQ, CBP, ABC, and PBQ and add the equations.

questions.q: In Triangle ABC, Angle A is twice Angle B ($A = 2B$). A point D lies on side AC such that BD bisects Angle B. If CD = 4 cm and AD = 3 cm, find the length of side AB.
questions.explanation: Triangle ABD is isosceles ($AD=BD=3$). Similarity or angle-bisector properties reveal $AB = CD + AD = 4 + 3 = 7$ cm.
